Then he stood in the courtroom’s prisoner’s box and turned to look at the gallery of about 25 officers, many in uniform, there in support of their colleague, Karl Brown, who was nearly stabbed to death during a wellness check two years ago in a downtown Sarnia condo building. Article content The officers didn’t audibly react to Whiteway’s comments, but a couple of soft claps could be heard as Justice Mark Poland found him guilty of both charges he was facing, attempted murder and aggravated assault, and again after the judge dismissed a pair of charter challenges the defence had raised in hopes of having the charges stayed . Whiteway, 37, who was denied bail and has been behind bars for two years, is expected to be sentenced early next year. Article content Ryan Whiteway appears in a Sarnia courtroom by video link from the Sarnia Jail shortly after his arrest in August 2024. Whiteway was convicted Tuesday of attempted murder and aggravated assault in the stabbing of a Sarnia police constable in a downtown condo building on Aug. 20, 2024. (Charles Vincent/Special to Postmedia Network) ‘EMOTIONAL’ REACTION TO VERDICT Brown, after exchanging hugs with several co-workers in the lobby, declined to comment on the outcome. His parents, Fred and Kathy, didn’t want to speak on his behalf, but observed this has weighed heavily on him. “It’s been tough,” Fred Brown said. “It’s a lot of weight off. Emotional,” said a choked-up Reg Musclow, a Sarnia police detective and close friend of Brown’s. Deputy Chief Mike Van Sickle said he was happy for Brown and called the trial part of the healing process. “Although the physical injuries heal, the traumatic effect of an incident like this will last – it could be forever, right? So it’s good that this part is done and the healing can continue,” he said. Article content Detective constables Karl Brown, left, and Erik Ostenfeldt with Sarnia police are shown at the Ontario Medal for Police Bravery ceremony in 2025. Handout ‘HARD FOR HIM TO HEAR’ Whiteway’s lawyer, Nicole DeBellefeuille, said her client maintains what he testified at trial: he thought someone broke into his condo, he didn’t know it was the police, and he wasn’t trying to kill anyone. “It was hard for him to hear that everything he said was rejected,” she said of the judge’s findings. DeBellefeuille said she expected they’d be at the Appeal Court on the issue. She also said she was “particularly shocked” about the findings on their charter challenge and the police’s use of force. THE STABBING AT THE SEAWAY CENTRE On Aug. 20, 2024, Brown, then a 37-year-old Sarnia police constable, was attacked while checking on Whiteway’s well-being inside his 15th-floor Seaway Centre condo. He needed 100 stitches, four blood transfusions and surgery on his thumb. Whiteway, 37, was arrested that night and charged with attempted murder and aggravated assault. At trial, Whiteway testified he thought the officers were aliens there to abduct him. He said he was a paranoid hermit who used drugs such as crystal meth, hash, THC and shatter. When the bathroom door flew open amid the well-being check and a ray of light – Brown’s flashlight – was shone on him, he reached for a self-defence tool, a collector’s knife, and attacked the “entity.” Article content Whiteway was found fit to stand trial after a criminal responsibility assessment , which was ordered in late 2024. While testifying, he also denied wanting to kill Brown and said had he known it was law enforcement, he would have acted differently. He also alleged he was assaulted by three or four Sarnia police officers for five or 10 minutes in what he called a brutal beat-down after his arrest, and again in the back of a cruiser. A Sarnia police cruiser is parked outside the Seaway Centre in Sarnia on Aug. 21, 2024, the day after Sarnia police said one of their officers was stabbed multiple times in the head and neck during a welfare check. (Terry Bridge/Sarnia Observer) CLOSING AND STAY ARGUMENTS DeBellefeuille argued for a stay of the charges due to the alleged police assault. She also argued police had no right to enter her client’s unit and that he acted in self-defence. Prosecutor Nila Mulpuru countered there was no evidence multiple officers assaulted Whiteway and the evidence they did have didn’t support self-defence. She also pointed to exigent circumstances, which allows for searches without warrants to prevent imminent bodily harm. POLAND’S DECISION Poland, who heard the case over five days this summer without a jury, spent more than an hour Tuesday explaining his decisions to convict Whiteway and dismiss the charter challenges. He said this case was about why Whiteway stabbed Brown and what he intended, along with examining the assertion that police had used excessive force. Article content He broke it down into four main issues: ISSUE #1: LAWFUL AUTHORITY TO ENTER Poland found the police did not breach Whiteway’s charter rights by entering his condo without prior authorization. He explained the Crown had to prove on a balance of probabilities their entry was authorized by law and reasonable. In the end, he found their decision to enter Whiteway’s home was justified. He pointed out Whiteway was well-known to police and officers had attended three times by the time Brown and Erik Ostenfeldt, his partner for the well-being check, arrived. They also met with a well-placed source, a neighbour who called police concerned for Whiteway’s well-being after they heard painful, distressed screaming that suddenly stopped, before going to Whiteway’s unit. Poland said the officers waiting about 17 minutes for the master key from a staff member did not diminish the exigent circumstances. And after going inside, he found they did what was expected of them by going into the locked bathroom amid their concerns for his well-being. The judge also said police conduct must be assessed in the circumstances as they appeared at the time, not in hindsight. ISSUE #2: SELF-DEFENCE Poland said it was up to the Crown to neutralize the defence’s self-defence argument – and it did. Article content He pointed to part of the law that says the act committed must be reasonable in the circumstances. Poland said it wasn’t reasonable for Whiteway to stab Brown if he knew Brown was a police officer. The judge found Whiteway did know this, despite his repeated denials. Police had been at his door 22 times in the past, according to Whiteway’s own testimony, and he also recorded a video through the peephole that night, which shows Brown and Ostenfeldt wearing their uniforms. Whiteway can be heard saying, “Yeah, head out, boy,” after the staffer gives them the master key and, “It’s going to get rough in here, boy,” shortly before they enter. Poland said he found Whiteway was aware police were there and intended to enter and the video demonstrated he didn’t adopt a panic room mode in response to unknown attendants, as he had testified. An email Whiteway sent shortly before the clash also was important in ascertaining his state of knowledge as it included the phrase “unauthorized entry,” which points to his knowing it was police, Poland said. A Sarnia police cruiser is parked outside the Seaway Centre in Sarnia on Aug. 21, 2024, the day after Sarnia police said one of their officers was stabbed multiple times in the head and neck during a welfare check. Terry Bridge/Sarnia Observer/Postmedia Network Photo by Terry Bridge / Terry Bridge/The Observer ISSUE #3: INTENT TO MURDER The Crown also had to prove the specific intent to murder beyond a reasonable doubt, Poland explained. Once again, it did. The judge rejected Whiteway’s testimony that he just attacked at the light. He pointed out the majority of the blows were inflicted on the vital and exposed parts of Brown’s body, such as his head and neck. He also used army-style knives and the element of surprise and stabbed from a position of tactical advantage. Article content After reviewing all the evidence, Poland said he was left without reasonable doubt Whiteway intended to murder Brown and convicted him. “I’m not going back to school for police foundations,” Whiteway uttered from the prisoner’s box in response. ISSUE #4: CRUEL AND UNUSUAL PUNISHMENT As for the cruel and unusual punishment charter argument, Poland said after rejecting Whiteway’s testimony he was left with no evidence that happened. Photos of damaged drywall with blood stains in his unit were not sufficient on their own. Poland noted Ostenfeldt had Brown’s blood mainly on the back of his uniform and there could have been incidental blood transfer on the wall. All of the officers denied assaulting Whiteway and the judge rejected Whiteway’s assertion he was beaten by three to four officers over five to 10 minutes. Sgt. Josh Mitchell testified a handcuffed Whiteway resisted arrest while he was briefly in a one-in-one situation with him and he had to turn custody over to other officers, worrying he would lose control after seeing his close friend, Brown, hurt and possibly dying. But Mitchell said he did not recall punching Whiteway or damaging the drywall. Poland noted Whiteway did not link any of the damage to the one-on-one encounter with Mitchell, just to an alleged group beat-down, which the judge said clearly did not occur. Article content The judge did say he found it unusual Mitchell was the only officer who said Whiteway resisted and that he directed the other officers out of the unit and was left alone with him. He added he had significant concerns about Mitchell’s reliability and credibility, raising questions about the precise nature of the application of force that did occur. But, with Whiteway’s credibility and reliability sorely imperiled, he was left with no evidence that Whiteway was assaulted. Whiteway also failed to point out any physical characteristics of the officer who allegedly punched him in the back of the cruiser, despite being in close proximity, the judge said. ‘WELL-ARTICULATED’ JUDGEMENT Van Sickle called Poland’s decision a well-articulated, well-researched and methodical evaluation of the evidence. “So I was very appreciative of that,” the deputy chief said. As for the assault allegations against their officers, Musclow said DeBellefeuille is a tenacious, very good defence lawyer who went over everything with a fine-tooth comb. “As you saw in the verdict from the judge, they were unfounded,” Musclow added. Mitchell and Ostenfeldt declined comment after the verdict. tbridge@postmedia.com Article content Share this article in your social network Share this Story : London Free Press Copy Link Email X Reddit Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Comments You must be logged in to join the discussion or read more comments. Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Community members hold photographs of loved ones during a vigil following the fatal chemical storage tank failure in Longview, Washington, on 26 May. Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images American crossroads Washington state After a deadly paper mill explosion, a community in Washington state looks to a key House race In a district shaken by the deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seat Lok Darjee Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On a misty morning in May in south-west Washington state , Laura Oltmann, a 41-year-old dietitian, had barely clocked in when an unfamiliar overhead announcement echoed through the hospital. “We get overhead pages for different types of emergencies. But this one, we don’t get very often,” recalled Oltmann. Doctors, nurses and staff began guessing what could have happened. Perhaps it was a train derailment. Maybe a major highway crash. As the speculation grew, so did the uncertainty. Staff started calling one another. The answer shook them all. “Someone mentioned there had been an explosion at this plant, and that we were probably going to be getting some patients from there,” Oltmann said. Forty miles south, in the port city of Longview, residents had awakened to a thunderous boom. At approximately 7.18am, as workers changed shifts at a paper mill company, Nippon Dynawave Packaging , a tank of white liquor, a caustic chemical used in the paper-making process, imploded. Hours passed with no explanation of what had caused it or how it could have happened at all, and suspicion began to brew. With roughly a thousand people working at the mill, thousands more were waiting for a phone call. Parents called children. Wives called husbands. Grandparents called grandchildren. View image in fullscreen Damage at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging mill in Longview, Washington, after an implosion on 26 May. Photograph: Karen Ducey/The Seattle Times/AP “For those that did not get that response,” said Jeff Wilson , a Republican state senator representing Longview, who also sits as the port commissioner, “all they got was silence.” In the end, 11 people were killed in one of Washington state’s deadliest industrial accidents in nearly a century. Nowhere was that impact felt more deeply than in Longview itself, a working-class city of about 38,000 people whose economy and identity have long been tied to the paper industry, shipping and logging. For generations, families have depended on the mills for their livelihoods. The disaster struck at something the city had long regarded as permanent: the mills where generations had gone to work, and helped many send their children to college or put down a down payment on a home. The implosion rippled through nearly every corner of a community affected by mill closures and economic change. Those concerns will likely have an impact at the ballot box. As summer turned toward fall and the leaves along the Columbia River began to turn yellow, memorial services gave way to campaign rallies. The same communities that had gathered around grieving families were preparing for one of the country’s most closely watched House races in November. Nearly two months after the implosion, on 8 July, Wilson still spoke first about the workers, the funerals he had attended, the families and the co-workers who ran toward danger looking for one another. He recalled brothers Tyler and Brad Covington , 27 and 29; he said: “They went to work together. And then they died together.” Before entering politics, Wilson spent more than 23 years cleaning tanks at the Nippon Dynawave mill. In the aftermath of the tragedy, he worked routinely with Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez ’s office as local, state and federal officials responded to the disaster, his role in Olympia intersecting with hers in Washington. View image in fullscreen Marie Gluesenkamp Perez speaks to reporters. Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images Though he declined to endorse her re-election, Wilson credited the Democratic congresswoman with being “present and accountable” and praised her for asking questions rather than “rubber-stamping anything”. For a community divided by many of the same political forces pulling at the rest of the country, the disaster briefly created a sense of togetherness, as the whole community grieved the deaths of many of their neighbor and family members. “Natural disasters will tend to bring people together,” said Mark Alan Smith, a political science professor at the University of Washington who studies American politics and religion. “It’s something people can unify around … across race and class and other divisions.” O n 4 August, Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican state senator John Braun advanced from a field of nine to face off for the district’s congressional seat in November. Braun finished first with about 39.7% of the vote to Gluesenkamp Perez’s 36.4% . Brent Hennrich, the progressive Democrat who argued that Gluesenkamp Perez no longer represented many of her party’s voters, took 16.7% . The results exposed the competing pressures facing Gluesenkamp Perez heading into the general election. Braun finished ahead of the incumbent, while Hennrich’s showing demonstrated the size of the progressive bloc she will have to contend with in November. Many of those voters remain angry over parts of her vote on the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (Save) Act (which would require proof of citizenship to vote), ICE funding and a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity. When asked about those direct criticisms of the congresswoman – whom many on the left feel has drifted from the party – her campaign responded with a written statement to the Guardian that cast her independence as the reason south-west Washington should return her to office. “DC has enough career politicians following national agendas,” said campaign manager Timothy Gowen. “Southwest Washington deserves an independent representative who delivers real results. Marie will always be loyal to her district first.” The statement did not address questions about her voting record or the primary result. View image in fullscreen John Braun at the capitol in Olympia last year. Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/AP The race stretches far beyond Longview and the nearby city of Battle Ground. Washington’s third congressional district runs from the Pacific coast through the timber towns of the lower Columbia and inland farm country to Vancouver and the fast-growing suburbs north of Portland. Logging, paper mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life across much of it, while its politics pull hard in opposite directions. That geography has forced Gluesenkamp Perez to build an unusual coalition. Her political survival has depended partly on voters who do not ordinarily identify with Democrats , including moderates and conservatives drawn to her emphasis on the trades, guns and independence from her party. But that same positioning has alienated Democrats who believe she has moved too far from them. “Two years ago, people reported having to hold their nose and vote for her, because she was better than [former opponent and one-time counter-intelligence official] Joe Kent,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. “But now we’re in a situation where I’m hearing from so many people that even if she wins the primary, they will not vote for her. And the frustration is real. I’m feeling that personally.” Thea Zaine, chair of the 20th Legislative District Democrats, speaks for the bloc of progressive Democrats whose discontent showed up in the primary returns. Her organization was the only Democratic party body in the district to endorse Hennrich. “We believe in protecting immigrants. She’s voted to give more money to ICE,” Zaine said. “She voted to give funding to wars in Iran. And she takes money from Aipac, and she’s voted to fund the genocide in Gaza. She voted against the war powers resolution to rein in Trump.” For Zaine, those votes have made the choice straightforward. But not every young, left-leaning voter who shares her frustration has reached the same conclusion. Tanner Manley, 25, an incoming law student who lives near Vancouver and describes himself as left-leaning, shares much of the critique. He plans to vote for Gluesenkamp Perez anyway. View image in fullscreen Protesters gather in front of the Henry M Jackson federal building in Seattle. Photograph: Rio Giancarlo/Getty Images “Of course, I wish more progressive candidates were viable here, and that Marie would take a clear moral stand on Israel and reject Aipac funding the way she refuses corporate Pac money,” he said. “In another race with different options, I’d likely support a different candidate.” What keeps Manley with her is closer to home. After the Longview disaster, the US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, the independent federal agency investigating the tank failure at the Longview paper plant, faced elimination under the administration’s proposed budget. In June, Gluesenkamp Perez backed an amendment restoring $14m for the agency , which passed the House appropriations committee with Republican support. “That might not satisfy progressives watching from the other side of the country,” Manley said, “but try telling people in this district that that kind of fight in Congress doesn’t matter.” Neither candidate’s campaign has made the Longview tragedy a centerpiece of the race. A recent poll underscores how little room both candidates have: the survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting , found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided. Smith, of the University of Washington, said events that bring communities together can be difficult to translate into partisan advantage. “In order for something like that to affect how people vote, somebody has to channel it,” Smith said. “It’s hard to channel anything where everybody agrees.” That could change, he said, “if you can somehow link your opponent to some negative aspect” of the event. So far, neither campaign has done so. And Wilson praised Gluesenkamp Perez’s handling of the disaster. “She’s been representing, you know, from the federal angle, well on this,” he said. The response also fit the political identity Gluesenkamp Perez has cultivated in south-west Washington, where she has emphasized the trades and the economic pressures facing rural and working-class communities. In an interview with OPB , she described watching the decline of industries that have long sustained towns across the region. “Mill after mill close in our region,” she said. “It’s just got people really at high anxiety levels.” A recent poll underscores how little room both House candidates have. The survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting , found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided. About three miles north of Nippon Dynawave, at the Pentecostal church where Ron Peterson is pastor, the disaster remains part of the community’s memory. For Peterson, 38, the tragedy had briefly brought together people who otherwise disagreed about much else. But when I asked him about politics, he drew a distinction. View image in fullscreen A vigil for the victims of the explosion. Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters “We don’t win politically,” he said. “We win spiritually.” A few miles south, and across a district where the divisions are not only political, Chydell Armijo, 35, mother of two, was thinking about something more immediate. She had little enthusiasm for either political party. What worried her was whether people like her could still build a stable life: whether a small business could survive, whether her children could find opportunity and whether working people could still move up. “I honestly feel like everybody is struggling,” Armijo said. “There is no such thing as middle class any more.” For all the attention on which party will control this congressional seat after November, Armijo saw a divide that would remain regardless of who won. “Our economic system has become difficult, in many ways, for us to climb,” she said. Finance Minister Taurimas Valys pledged continued support for Ukraine’s victory and reconstruction. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 8, 2026, 7:14 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) and Lithuania’s President Gitanas Nauseda (L) shake hands during Nordic-Baltic Eight summit in Kyiv on August 23, 2026. (Photo by Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Lithuania’s government approved an additional €15 million ($16.8 million) in financial assistance to Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7, directing the funds through the World Bank and European Investment Bank (EIB) to support reconstruction and strengthen the country’s economic resilience amid Russia’s ongoing war. According to Lithuania’s Ministry of Finance, €10 million ($11.2 million) will go to the World Bank’s Special Program for Ukraine Recovery 2.0 (SPUR 2.0), while €5 million ($5.6 million) will be allocated to the EIB’s EU for Ukraine Fund (EU4U). JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Lithuanian Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said continued assistance was essential not only for Ukraine’s survival but also for Europe’s security. Advertisement “Today, Ukrainians are fighting not only for their own freedom but for ours as well. Uninterrupted and timely support is the least we must provide. It is our duty to ensure that Ukraine has everything it needs – both to achieve victory and to rebuild the country,” Valys said. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha welcomed the decision, thanking Lithuania for its continued commitment to Ukraine. “Thank you, Lithuania, for another €15 million for Ukraine’s recovery and resilience through the World Bank and EIB mechanisms,” Sybiha wrote on X . “Lithuania has stood shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine from the very beginning,” he added, praising Vilnius for practical decisions that help Ukraine recover and grow stronger. Other Topics of Interest Sine Engineering Appoints Mykolska as VP of Growth and Affairs Ukrainian defense startup Sine Engineering taps Nataliya Mykolska as VP of growth and affairs to lead international expansion and attract capital. Funding Ukraine’s recovery and reconstruction The €10 million ($11.2 million) contribution to SPUR 2.0 will support a World Bank financing mechanism designed to mobilize additional resources for Ukraine’s recovery. Established in June 2026, the program allows donor contributions to generate approximately three times their value in concessional lending. According to Lithuania’s Finance Ministry, $2 billion in donor contributions could unlock around $6 billion in loans to Ukraine on favorable terms. Advertisement The program also includes a private-sector component aimed at encouraging investment and supporting Ukraine’s economic recovery. Lithuania previously contributed €10 million ($11.2 million at the Oct. 7, 2026 exchange rate) to the original SPUR program in 2023. The remaining €5 million ($5.6 million) will go to the EIB’s EU4U Fund, which finances critical infrastructure reconstruction and projects strengthening Ukraine’s economic resilience. The EIB requested additional contributions from member states in July after previously committed funding for Ukrainian projects was nearly exhausted. Lithuania also contributed €10 million to the EU4U Fund in 2023. Lithuania reaffirms long-term commitment to Ukraine Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Lithuania’s Finance Ministry has allocated more than €93 million ($104.2 million) to Ukraine through international financial institutions and EU mechanisms, alongside €26 million ($29.1 million) in bilateral assistance. Valys said Ukraine’s financial requirements and the international community’s continued assistance would be among the central issues discussed at next week’s annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. Advertisement During a September meeting with Ukrainian Ambassador Olha Nikitchenko, Valys said Ukraine’s security was inseparable from Europe’s and reaffirmed that assistance to Kyiv would remain a priority during Lithuania’s presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027.
